# Day 7: Protein Structure

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to describe the four
levels of protein structure, use PyMOL to load and inspect a real
structure, and explain why predicting the tertiary (3D) fold from
sequence alone is a harder problem than the secondary-structure
prediction Day 6 already introduced.

## The four levels of protein structure

A protein starts as a **polypeptide chain**: a linear polymer of amino
acids, connected head-to-tail, that only becomes a functional protein
once it folds up in water. Structural biology describes that folded
result at four increasingly complex levels:

- **Primary structure** — the sequence of amino acids itself, exactly
  the object Days 1-6 have been aligning, scoring, and classifying. No
  3D information yet.
- **Secondary structure** — local, repeating backbone shapes, already
  introduced narratively on Day 6: the **alpha helix**, a coil held
  together by hydrogen bonds between backbone N-H and C=O groups four
  residues apart, and the **beta sheet**, built from extended **beta
  strands** hydrogen-bonded edge to edge with their neighbors. Anything
  that's neither is usually just called **coil**.
- **Tertiary structure** — how those secondary-structure elements, and
  everything connecting them, pack together into one compact 3D shape
  for a single chain. This is held together mostly by the
  **hydrophobic effect** (water excludes non-polar side chains from its
  surface, driving them to bury themselves inside the fold) plus
  weaker non-covalent forces between atoms of the backbone and side
  chains (hydrogen bonds, electrostatic attraction between charged side
  chains, and van der Waals contacts).
- **Quaternary structure** — how multiple, separately-folded chains
  arrange themselves with respect to each other into one functional
  assembly. Not every protein has this level at all (many function as
  a single chain); those that do can range from two chains up to,
  in some experimentally solved structures, hundreds.

**A real example, continuing this course's running case study.**
Hemoglobin is a **heterotetramer**: two copies of an alpha-globin chain
(141 residues) and two copies of *HBB*, beta-globin (146 residues, this
course's running example since Day 3), each chain independently folded
and each carrying its own oxygen-binding heme group. The notebook
re-derives — independently of Day 6's PDBe API lookup, using a different
tool (PyMOL's own `dss` algorithm) — that one beta chain is **118 of 146
residues (80.8%) alpha helix, 0% beta strand**, confirming Day 6's number
by a second, unrelated computational method rather than just repeating
it. Rendering all four chains together, colored separately, with the
four hemes shown as spheres, makes tertiary and quaternary structure
directly visible at once:

![PDB entry `2HHB`, human deoxyhemoglobin: two alpha chains (blue/cyan),
two beta chains (salmon/pink), four heme iron atoms (orange spheres).
Rendered from the real structure with PyMOL, not
illustrated.](figs/day07-hemoglobin-tetramer.png){width=85%}

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Protein structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein_structure) — a fuller treatment of all four levels
- RCSB [PDB-101](https://pdb101.rcsb.org/) — short, illustrated explainers on structure and specific proteins, aimed at newcomers

## Protein domain classification

A **domain** is a compact, semi-independent unit within a tertiary
structure — often able to fold and function on its own even when cut
out of the rest of the chain, and frequently reused across otherwise
unrelated proteins as a kind of structural building block. Days 3 and 5
already covered domains from the *sequence* side (InterPro/Pfam, built
from profile HMMs over sequence alignments). The databases below
classify domains the other way round — from the actual solved 3D shape
— which can group together real structural relatives that sequence
alone misses entirely (sequence similarity fades away long before
structural similarity does), and can equally miss a real relationship
sequence-based methods do catch. Four real classification databases,
each with a genuinely different philosophy:

- **SCOP** (Structural Classification of Proteins; Murzin et al., 1995)
  — the original: a hierarchy (class → fold → superfamily → family)
  built mostly by expert manual curation, prioritizing classification
  accuracy over automated coverage of every solved structure. Hosted at
  EBI: [`ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/scop`](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/scop/).
- **CATH** (Class, Architecture, Topology, Homologous superfamily;
  Orengo et al., 1997) — a parallel hierarchy with a similar spirit but
  a different, more automated pipeline and different boundary/grouping
  decisions in practice. [`cathdb.info`](https://www.cathdb.info/).
- **ECOD** (Evolutionary Classification of Domains; Cheng et al., 2014)
  — organizes domains primarily by inferred evolutionary relationship
  rather than pure structural similarity, explicitly built to separate
  "related by common ancestry" from "similar by coincidence or
  convergence."
  [`prodata.swmed.edu/ecod`](http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod/).
- **TED** (The Encyclopedia of Domains; Lau, Bordin et al., 2024, from
  the same group that maintains CATH) — the newest of the four, built
  by algorithmically parsing essentially the *entire* AlphaFold
  Structure Database into domains at a scale no manual curation effort
  could reach: hundreds of millions of predicted structures, not just
  the roughly 200,000 experimentally solved ones the other three draw
  from. [`ted.cathdb.info`](https://ted.cathdb.info/).

These four don't always agree with each other on exactly where one
domain ends and the next begins, or on how to group distant
superfamilies together — a genuine, long-standing methodological
tension in the field (different curation philosophies and similarity
thresholds), not a matter of one being simply "right" and the others
"wrong." Knowing more than one of these exists, and why, matters more
than picking a single favorite.

## Why predicting the fold from sequence is hard

A given amino acid sequence reliably folds into the same 3D structure
every time under normal cellular conditions — this observation is often
called **Anfinsen's dogma**, after Christian Anfinsen's experiments
showing a denatured (unfolded) protein could refold correctly entirely on
its own, with no other machinery needed. That implies all the
information needed to determine the fold is, in principle, already
present in the sequence.

In principle is the operative phrase: reliably *predicting* that fold
computationally, starting from sequence alone, has been one of
biology's hardest open problems for decades. Three classical strategies
were developed, each with a real limitation:

- **De novo (ab initio) modeling** — simulate the physics directly:
  fold the chain by searching for the arrangement with the lowest free
  energy. The most rigorous approach in principle, but computationally
  so expensive it was, for a long time, only practical for small
  proteins (under roughly 100 residues). **Rosetta** (Baker lab,
  University of Washington) is the best-known real software built
  around exactly this approach — originally assembling structures from
  short fragments of similar, already-solved sequences rather than
  searching the full physical space from nothing, later extended well
  beyond ab initio prediction into comparative modeling and protein
  *design* (building a new sequence to fold into a chosen shape, not
  just predicting the fold of an existing one). David Baker shared the
  2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work — alongside Demis
  Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold, the deep-learning method
  below — a real, direct link between this session's "classical" and
  "modern" strategies, not two unrelated stories.
- **Comparative modeling (homology modeling / threading)** — if a
  protein of known structure is similar enough in sequence, assume the
  new protein folds the same way and build a model from that template.
  Cheap and reliable when a good template exists, but structurally
  useless for a genuinely new fold with no close relative already
  solved.
- **Evolutionary (contact-based) methods** — infer which residue pairs
  are likely to be physically close in the folded structure from
  patterns of co-evolution across many homologous sequences in a
  multiple alignment. This is the same evolutionary information Day 5's
  profiles and PSSMs are built from, now used for a 3D geometric
  question rather than a purely sequence-based score — a second,
  independent instance of "evolutionary information helps," one level up
  in structural complexity from Day 6's secondary-structure example.

None of these three classical strategies solved the general problem
reliably. The real breakthrough came from a fourth strategy — deep
learning, most famously AlphaFold (2020) — which Day 12 covers properly,
once this course has built up the neural-network machinery (Days 6-9)
that made it possible.

## Comparing structures: RMSD, TM-score, and Foldseek

Structures need to be **compared** to each other quantitatively, not
just predicted — e.g. to check how close a predicted structure is to
the real one, or whether two real structures share a fold at all.

**RMSD** (root-mean-square deviation) is the most direct measure: after
optimally superimposing two structures, it's the root-mean-square
distance between their corresponding atoms. Simple, but sensitive to
protein length and to a single badly-misplaced loop dragging the whole
number up even when the rest of the fold matches well. The **TM-score**
fixes both problems with a length-normalizing formula that also
down-weights small local deviations, giving a score from 0 to 1 that's
comparable across proteins of different sizes — roughly, above ~0.5
indicates the same overall fold, and 1.0 is a perfect match.

**Foldseek** (van Kempen, Steinegger et al., 2024) does for structure
search what BLAST (Day 5) does for sequence search: turn database-scale
structural comparison from something expensive into something that
runs in seconds. Its key idea is a change of representation, the same
kind of move that makes BLAST fast — it encodes each residue's local
3D neighborhood into a small discrete "3Di" alphabet, so comparing two
*structures* becomes comparing two *strings* with fast sequence-alignment
methods instead of expensive geometric superposition. This is what
makes it practical to search a single query against the hundreds of
millions of structures in the AlphaFold Structure Database and the PDB
combined, in seconds rather than days. Before Foldseek, **DALI** (Holm
& Sander, 1993) and **TM-align** (Zhang & Skolnick, 2005) were the
standard tools for exactly this kind of comparison — both real,
accurate, and still used for a single careful pairwise alignment, just
far too slow to run at Foldseek's database scale.

**A real worked comparison**, run locally with Foldseek on three real
structures: the two hemoglobin states already used on this page
(`2HHB`, `1HHO`) plus a real, unrelated fold, green fluorescent protein
(`1EMA`, an all-beta barrel — nothing like hemoglobin's all-alpha
globin fold). Matching alpha-to-alpha or beta-to-beta chains between
`2HHB` and `1HHO` (the *same* protein in two conformational states)
gives a TM-score of **0.98** and an RMSD of **0.7 Å** — about as similar
as two independently solved structures get. Comparing across chain
types (alpha vs. beta globin — related by evolution, but only ~43%
identical in sequence) still gives a TM-score around **0.90-0.91**
(RMSD ~1.7-1.8 Å) — the fold stays clearly recognizable as the same
globin family even once sequence identity has dropped a long way,
exactly the "structure is more conserved than sequence" point Day 5's
evolutionary methods rely on, now shown geometrically rather than
asserted. Searching `2HHB` against GFP (`1EMA`) returns **zero hits**,
even with an artificially loosened significance threshold — Foldseek
correctly finds no meaningful structural relationship between two
genuinely unrelated folds.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root-mean-square_deviation_of_atomic_positions) and [Template modeling score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template_modeling_score)
- Foldseek, [GitHub](https://github.com/steineggerlab/foldseek) and [web server](https://search.foldseek.com/search) — try it on any real PDB entry or AlphaFold model, no installation needed

## Structure visualization: PyMOL

[PyMOL](https://pymol.org/) is one of the two most widely used molecular
visualization programs in structural biology (alongside ChimeraX),
free and open-source. It loads a structure directly from a PDB entry,
renders it in several standard representations — **cartoon** (secondary
structure as ribbons/arrows/coils, used for the figure above), **sticks**
(every bond drawn explicitly, useful for a single side chain or ligand),
and **spheres** (every atom as a ball, useful for packing/space-filling
views) — and can measure real geometric quantities (distances, angles)
directly from the loaded coordinates by clicking on atoms or via its
command line. Today's lab uses it hands-on; the notebook drives the same
program headlessly from Python to make its figures and measurements
reproducible outside the interactive GUI. (Biopython, introduced on Day
2 for sequences, also has a structure-handling module, `Bio.PDB` — this
course uses PyMOL instead, for its fuller visualization and analysis
toolkit.)

## The notebook

`notebooks/day07-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb` fetches two real
hemoglobin structures — deoxygenated `2HHB` and oxygenated `1HHO` — and
uses them to make every level of structure concrete: primary and
quaternary structure from simply parsing chains, secondary structure
independently cross-checked against Day 6's number using PyMOL's own
algorithm, and a real measured quaternary-structure distance (the
iron-to-iron distance between the two beta hemes) that changes by about
5 Å between the two states — a genuine, measured instance of
hemoglobin's textbook allosteric mechanism (Baldwin & Chothia, 1979), not
just a diagram. Open it in
[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day07-protein-structure-in-code.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.

## The lab

**Full lab, PyMOL-first**, across three real structures beyond this
page's own hemoglobin example: a real HIV envelope glycoprotein
trimer/antibody complex (`7LXM`) for representations, chain coloring,
extracting objects, structural alignment (`cealign`), and finding a
real sequence inside a structure; a real chitinase with real bound
metal ions and an inhibitor (`8C6Z`) for selecting and visualizing
charged residues; and human neuroglobin (`1OJ6`) for a real Foldseek/
TM-score comparison (in
[`notebooks/day07-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day07-lab.ipynb))
against its own real AlphaFold DB prediction, a related real globin,
and an unrelated real fold — plus a real domain-classification lookup
in CATH, tying back to this page's own new sections. Viewing a
structure directly in VS Code (via the real Protein Viewer extension,
handy while connected to the shared course server over SSH) is also
covered.

## What's next

Day 8 moves from a single yes/no output (Day 6's XOR problem) to
multi-class prediction — softmax regression — and from raw
tensors to a properly structured PyTorch model, using a real multi-class
biological problem (subcellular localization) as the case study. Day 9
comes back to deliver Rost & Sander's PHD method in full, now that both
the hidden-layer motivation (Day 6) and the tools to build one properly
(Day 8) are in place.
